questions.prompt: What does the depletion approximation assume about the PN junction?
options: Within \(-x_p < x < x_n\), all free carriers are removed, so \(\rho = -qN_A\) on the P side and \(+qN_D\) on the N side; outside, the material is neutral
The carrier concentrations change linearly across the junction
The field is constant across the transition region
Only the minority carriers are depleted
questions.explanation:
Reader Eq. 5.27. Every 60 mV drop in potential cuts the carrier density by 10 times. After a few tenths of a volt the carriers are negligible next to the dopants, so treating the region as fully depleted is accurate.
The payoff: \(\rho\) becomes piecewise constant, so the field is piecewise linear and the potential piecewise quadratic, which is easy to solve.

questions.prompt: Find the total zero-bias depletion width \(X_{d0} = \sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon_s\varphi_{bi}}{q}\left(\frac{1}{N_A}+\frac{1}{N_D}\right)}\) for \(N_A = N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). (\(\varphi_{bi} = 0.718\ \mathrm{V}\), \(\varepsilon_s = 11.7\varepsilon_0 = 1.036\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/cm}\), \(q = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\).) Answer in µm.
questions.explanation:
\[X_{d0} = \sqrt{\frac{2(1.036\times10^{-12})(0.718)}{1.602\times10^{-19}}\left(2\times10^{-16}\right)} = 4.31\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm} \approx 0.431\ \mu\mathrm{m}\]
Half on each side for a symmetric junction. Keep everything in cm: \(\varepsilon_s\) in F/cm and \(N\) in cm⁻³ give \(X\) in cm. Then convert (\(1\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 10^{-4}\) cm).

questions.prompt: Under the depletion approximation, what does the electric field look like across the junction?
options: Constant across the depletion region and zero outside
Largest at the depletion edges and zero at the junction
Exponentially decaying away from the junction
Piecewise linear: zero at both depletion edges and largest in magnitude at the metallurgical junction (a triangle)
questions.explanation:
\(dE/dx = \rho/\varepsilon_s\) is constant on each side, so \(E\) is linear. It starts at 0 at \(-x_p\) and reaches \(-qN_Ax_p/\varepsilon_s\) at \(x = 0\) (Eq. 5.30), then returns to 0 at \(x_n\).
Gauss's law explains the peak: a box from the neutral P side to \(x\) encloses more and more negative charge until \(x = 0\); after that, positive charge starts cancelling it.

questions.prompt: A one-sided junction has \(N_A = 10^{18}\) and \(N_D = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), so \(\varphi_{bi} = 0.7783\ \mathrm{V}\). Using \(x_n = \sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon_s\varphi_{bi}}{q}\cdot\frac{N_A}{N_D(N_A+N_D)}}\), find \(x_n\) in µm. (\(\varepsilon_s = 1.036\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/cm}\))
questions.explanation:
\[x_n = \sqrt{\frac{2(1.036\times10^{-12})(0.7783)}{1.602\times10^{-19}}\cdot\frac{10^{18}}{10^{15}(1.001\times10^{18})}} = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm} \approx 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}\]
Since \(N_A \gg N_D\), this is almost \(\sqrt{2\varepsilon_s\varphi_{bi}/(qN_D)}\) (reader Eq. 5.38–5.39): the lightly doped side holds nearly all the depletion width.

questions.prompt: For the same junction (\(N_D = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(x_n = 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}\)), what is the peak field magnitude \(|E_{max}| = qN_Dx_n/\varepsilon_s\)? Answer in kV/cm.
questions.explanation:
\[|E_{max}| = \frac{qN_Dx_n}{\varepsilon_s} = \frac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{15})(10^{-4})}{1.036\times10^{-12}} \approx 1.55\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/cm}\]
That is about 15.5 kV/cm. You'd get the same answer from the P side, \(qN_Ax_p/\varepsilon_s\), because \(N_Ax_p = N_Dx_n\): the field is continuous at the junction (Eq. 5.33).

questions.prompt: Same junction: how wide is the P-side depletion region, \(x_p\), in nm? (Use \(N_Ax_p = N_Dx_n\) with \(x_n = 1.003\ \mu\mathrm{m}\).)
questions.explanation:
\[x_p = x_n\frac{N_D}{N_A} = 1.003\ \mu\mathrm{m}\times10^{-3} \approx 1\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Under a nanometre: the heavily doped side barely depletes at all. That's why a P⁺N junction is analysed as 'one-sided'.

questions.prompt: In a junction with \(N_A = 10^{17}\) and \(N_D = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), which side has the wider depletion region, and why?
options: The P side, because higher doping produces more charge
Both are equal, because the junction is neutral
The N side (lightly doped): it has fewer ions per volume, so it must deplete a longer distance to uncover the same charge
The P side, because holes diffuse farther than electrons
questions.explanation:
Neutrality of the whole dipole: \(N_Ax_p = N_Dx_n\), so \(x_n/x_p = N_A/N_D = 100\).
Gotcha: the heavily doped side has MORE charge per volume, so it needs LESS width. Equal TOTAL charge on each side doesn't mean equal width.

questions.prompt: In a junction the peak field magnitude is \(|E_{max}| = 50\ \mathrm{kV/cm}\) and the total depletion width is \(X_d = 0.3\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). What potential difference is dropped across the depletion region?
questions.explanation:
The potential drop is the area under the field. The field is a triangle with base \(X_d\) and height \(|E_{max}|\):
\[\Delta\varphi = \tfrac12|E_{max}|X_d = \tfrac12(5\times10^{4})(0.3\times10^{-4}) = 0.75\ \mathrm{V}\]
Gotcha: forgetting the ½ (getting 1.5 V) treats the field as constant. This handy relation gives \(|E_{max}| = 2\varphi_{bi}/X_d\) in reverse.

questions.prompt: In an asymmetric junction (\(N_A = 10\,N_D\)), how is the built-in potential split between the P-side and N-side parts of the depletion region?
options: Most of it falls on the lightly doped N side: φ_N : φ_P = N_A : N_D = 10 : 1
Most falls on the heavily doped P side, in the ratio 10 : 1
It all falls exactly at the metallurgical junction
questions.explanation:
Each side's drop is a triangle area: \(\varphi_N = \tfrac12|E_{max}|x_n\) and \(\varphi_P = \tfrac12|E_{max}|x_p\), with the same peak field. So \(\varphi_N/\varphi_P = x_n/x_p = N_A/N_D\).
Gotcha: the lightly doped side takes both the width and the voltage. That's why, in a one-sided junction (and in the MOS body), you analyse only the lightly doped side.

questions.prompt: Preview of reverse bias: an applied reverse voltage \(V_R\) adds to the junction's potential step, so \(\varphi_{bi}\) becomes \(\varphi_{bi} + V_R\) in the width formula. For the symmetric \(10^{16}\) junction (\(\varphi_{bi} = 0.718\ \mathrm{V}\)), by what factor does the depletion width grow at \(V_R = 3\ \mathrm{V}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(X_d \propto \sqrt{\text{total potential}}\), so
\[\frac{X_d(3\ \mathrm{V})}{X_{d0}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.718 + 3}{0.718}} \approx 2.28\]
It's a square-root law: 5 times the voltage only about doubles the width. The reverse-bias skill builds on exactly this.

questions.prompt: Preview of junction capacitance: the depletion region acts like a parallel-plate capacitor with silicon as the dielectric, \(C = \varepsilon_s/X_d\) per unit area. Using \(X_{d0} = 0.431\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) for the symmetric \(10^{16}\) junction, what is \(C\) in fF/µm²?
questions.explanation:
\[C = \frac{\varepsilon_s}{X_{d0}} = \frac{1.036\times10^{-12}}{4.31\times10^{-5}} = 2.4\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{F/cm^2}\]
\(1\ \mathrm{F/cm^2} = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{fF}/10^{8}\ \mu\mathrm{m^2} = 10^{7}\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\), so \(C \approx 0.24\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\).
Because \(X_d\) changes with voltage, this capacitance does too: the basis of varactors and of the parasitic capacitances in transistors.

questions.prompt: Preview of the MOS capacitor: under a MOS gate, the p-type body depletes like the lightly doped side of a one-sided junction. If 0.5 V is dropped across a body with \(N_A = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), how deep is the depletion region, \(x_d = \sqrt{2\varepsilon_s\varphi/(qN_A)}\), in nm?
questions.explanation:
\[x_d = \sqrt{\frac{2(1.036\times10^{-12})(0.5)}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{17})}} = 8.04\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{cm} \approx 80.4\ \mathrm{nm}\]
The gate plays the role of the heavily doped side (a sheet of charge with zero width). The MOS skills use this result to find where the body depletes and when it inverts.
